power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Psychedelics, spirituality and drug policy: Harm reduction without compulsory medicalisation

author.affiliation:
Cerveau et Cognition (LMC2
								Laboratoire Mémoire
								
									7536)
									UR

text.text: Psychedelic experiences can be meaningful and beneficial, including outside clinical treatment.
They can also leave people distressed or vulnerable.
Spiritual interpretations of these experiences therefore raise a practical question for drug policy: how can people be protected while preserving legitimate uses beyond psychiatry?

Drawing on selected human studies and ethical and policy scholarship, this Commentary examines naturalistic benefits, mystical experiences, and concerns about spiritual bypassing and spiritual emergency, whose definitions and empirical support remain uneven.
We argue that uncertainty about these risks calls for prevention and proportionate safeguards, but does not, by itself, justify restricting access to psychiatric treatment.

We propose four priorities across clinical, community, and religious settings: meaningful consent, protection against exploitation, accessible support after use, and follow-up that records difficulties as well as benefits.
Particular attention should be paid to interpretive autonomy: people's freedom to understand and reconsider their experiences without pressure to adopt a provider's beliefs.

We claim that the notions of cognitive liberty and freedom of religion or belief strengthen the importance of scrutinising unnecessary restrictions, while retaining duties to prevent coercion and harm.
We propose that policy assessment should also include harms associated with prohibition.
The aim is to protect people during potentially valuable but vulnerable experiences, including those who seek meaning or well-being without a psychiatric diagnosis.
People use psychedelics for many reasons, including relief from suffering, curiosity, relationships, spiritual exploration, and religious practice.
Some uses have a long history, as illustrated by archaeological evidence of psychoactive plants in ritual contexts.
For example, chemical analyses of a ritual bundle from Bolivia, dated to approximately 1,000 years ago, identified dimethyltryptamine and harmine (Miller et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For example, chemical analyses of a ritual bundle from Bolivia, dated to approximately 1,000 years ago, identified dimethyltryptamine and harmine <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Miller et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This does not establish the safety of current practices, but it highlights that psychiatric treatment is one context within a much wider human relationship with these substances.
The limits of psychedelic medicalisation have already been examined by Noorani (2020), and Caraccio et al. (2025) have proposed ethical guidance spanning medical and non-medical uses.
text.formatted: The limits of psychedelic medicalisation have already been examined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Noorani (2020)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Caraccio et al. (2025)</ref> have proposed ethical guidance spanning medical and non-medical uses.

text.text: We build on this work by asking how evidence about benefits and difficulties associated with spiritually motivated use should inform prevention and access.
Mystical experiences have sometimes been associated with improvements in mental health.
At the same time, researchers have documented spiritual struggles, integration difficulties, and distress after psychedelic use (Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023; Schutt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: At the same time, researchers have documented spiritual struggles, integration difficulties, and distress after psychedelic use <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Schutt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In a recent cross-sectional survey of 147 Western psychedelic users, religiously or spiritually motivated users did not report greater suggestibility or subclinical psychotic experiences than users without these motivations (Fauvel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a recent cross-sectional survey of 147 Western psychedelic users, religiously or spiritually motivated users did not report greater suggestibility or subclinical psychotic experiences than users without these motivations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fauvel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are preliminary and do not settle questions about risk, yet, they do show why policy should ask what happens, to whom, and under which conditions, rather than treating spiritual use as inherently harmful.
If poorly understood, risks become sufficient grounds for reserving legitimate use to psychiatry, and uncertainty will have set an access rule before alternatives have been assessed.
This Commentary draws on selected human research, principally on psilocybin and ayahuasca.
We propose an approach we call accountable pluralism: different purposes and settings of psychedelic use may deserve recognition, with clear responsibilities for protecting participants.
Regarding benefits, naturalistic studies follow people who choose to use psychedelics outside a clinical trial.
Several prospective naturalistic studies report average improvements in symptoms or well-being (Mans et al., 2021; Nayak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Several prospective naturalistic studies report average improvements in symptoms or well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Mans et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Nayak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings point in a similar direction to some clinical results, although the populations, outcomes, and settings differ (Davis et al., 2021; Bogenschutz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These findings point in a similar direction to some clinical results, although the populations, outcomes, and settings differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Davis et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bogenschutz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, similar directions of change do not establish equivalent efficacy or safety.
It is also important to note that both naturalistic studies and clinical trials have limitations.
In Nayak et al. (2023) naturalistic study, only 657 of 2,833 baseline respondents completed the final assessment, and approximately half of those respondents had used psilocybin again.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Nayak et al. (2023)</ref> naturalistic study, only 657 of 2,833 baseline respondents completed the final assessment, and approximately half of those respondents had used psilocybin again.

text.text: Additional exposure and selective follow-up could therefore contribute to the reported changes.
Clinical trials can control dose and provide screening and support, but they recruit selected patients and may have difficulty maintaining blinding (Ross et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Clinical trials can control dose and provide screening and support, but they recruit selected patients and may have difficulty maintaining blinding <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ross et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Regarding setting, the context in which the psychedelics is taken also deserves attention.

In a small retreat study featuring experienced users and low alkaloid doses, depression, anxiety, and stress decreased by the following morning in both ayahuasca and placebo groups (Uthaug et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In a small retreat study featuring experienced users and low alkaloid doses, depression, anxiety, and stress decreased by the following morning in both ayahuasca and placebo groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Uthaug et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In an other experiment where 33 students received a placebo presented as a psychedelic in a party-like setting, many reported some drug-like effects (Olson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In an other experiment where 33 students received a placebo presented as a psychedelic in a party-like setting, many reported some drug-like effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Olson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These studies illustrate how expectations and social context may shape subjective reports.
Regarding safety, Psychedelics dangerosity requires more than a single reassuring or alarming label.
Psilocybin and LSD are generally described as having relatively low direct physiological toxicity at commonly studied doses (Nichols, 2016).
text.formatted: Psilocybin and LSD are generally described as having relatively low direct physiological toxicity at commonly studied doses <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Nichols, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, acute effects can include nausea, headache, anxiety, and increases in blood pressure, and low physiological toxicity does not exclude psychological harm.
Psychological safety includes both what happens during the experience and what follows.
Acute fear may resolve with support, whereas persistent distress or difficulties in integration and everyday functioning require attention after intoxication has ended.
Serious psychiatric events reported in the literature also warrant care, even where their frequency is uncertain.
The limitations in adverse-event monitoring identified by Hinkle et al. (2024) make it important to give people clear information about possible difficulties and routes to timely help.
text.formatted: The limitations in adverse-event monitoring identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hinkle et al. (2024)</ref> make it important to give people clear information about possible difficulties and routes to timely help.

text.text: Taken together, these findings justify studying the benefits and risks of psychedelic use in contexts where it already occurs.
They do not, however, establish the therapeutic effectiveness of psychedelics for any specific disorder.
This distinction matters for policy, as people may also value psychedelic experiences for reasons other than relief from illness, including meaning, connection, or personal exploration.
Such uses do not require a psychiatric diagnosis, although they remain subject to appropriate safeguards.
A mystical-type experience, a spiritual interpretation, and a religious identity are related but different things.
Someone may report unity or profound meaning without adopting a spiritual worldview.
A preregistered longitudinal study found no association between psychedelic use and changes in self-rated religiosity or spirituality over two months (Cherniak & Granqvist, 2025).
text.formatted: A preregistered longitudinal study found no association between psychedelic use and changes in self-rated religiosity or spirituality over two months <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cherniak & Granqvist, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, evidence that more intense mystical experiences predict better psychological outcomes is mixed.

For instance, in a small clinical follow-up, mystical and spiritual ratings correlated at twelve months with positive changes participants attributed to psilocybin, but not with improvement in clinician-rated depression (Gukasyan et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, in a small clinical follow-up, mystical and spiritual ratings correlated at twelve months with positive changes participants attributed to psilocybin, but not with improvement in clinician-rated depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gukasyan et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Even when a study finds a statistical link between mystical experience intensity and clinical outcomes, it cannot by itself show that the mystical experience caused the improvement, as expectations, support, and other features of the experience may shape both the rating and later outcomes.
A beneficial outcome therefore provides no general reason to require a spiritual explanation or to maximise mystical experience likelihood.
This is where interpretive autonomy becomes relevant: people should remain free to understand, question, and reconsider their own experiences.
On one side, Johnson (2021) warns against clinicians imposing their religious beliefs in psychedelic therapy.
text.formatted: On one side, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Johnson (2021)</ref> warns against clinicians imposing their religious beliefs in psychedelic therapy.

text.text: On the other side, Zeller (2025) likewise raises concerns about epistemic harm caused by secular psychedelic therapists and argues that people's ability to assess beliefs and make their own judgments deserves protection.
A powerful feeling of revelation need not settle whether a belief is true, and providers should leave room for reflection and alternative explanations.
Likewise, choosing a religious ceremony should not prevent someone from questioning a guide's interpretation or changing their mind.
Spiritual and secular interpretations both deserve respect, but neither should be imposed as a condition of receiving psychedelic care.
The concepts of spiritual bypassing and spiritual emergency should be refined and treated as separate concepts to not obscure their different implications for prevention.
Spiritual bypassing means using spiritual explanations or practices to avoid emotional difficulties, responsibilities, or needed help (Fox et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Spiritual bypassing means using spiritual explanations or practices to avoid emotional difficulties, responsibilities, or needed help <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fox et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In interviews with thirty retreat participants, nine spontaneously reported integration challenges that the authors described as transient and coexisting with reported benefits.
One participant explicitly described spiritual bypassing (Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023).
text.formatted: One participant explicitly described spiritual bypassing <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A recent cross-sectional survey also compared spiritual bypassing between religious, spiritual but not religious, and secular psychedelic users.
It shows that religiously motivated users reported higher spiritual bypassing scores, but with a positive association with well-being in this sample (Fauvel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: It shows that religiously motivated users reported higher spiritual bypassing scores, but with a positive association with well-being in this sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fauvel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Neither study estimates how common bypassing is in the wider population or shows that psychedelics caused it.

The term spiritual emergency offers a framework for understanding destabilising experiences as part of a spiritual transformation (Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023). Evans et al. (2023) documented anxiety, existential distress, and dissociative difficulties among people recruited specifically because they had experienced lasting difficulties after a psychedelic intake.
text.formatted: The term spiritual emergency offers a framework for understanding destabilising experiences as part of a spiritual transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lutkajtis & Evans, 2023)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Evans et al. (2023)</ref> documented anxiety, existential distress, and dissociative difficulties among people recruited specifically because they had experienced lasting difficulties after a psychedelic intake.

text.text: Practitioners also describe helping people who struggle with their sense of self or understanding of reality after psychedelic use (Argyri et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Practitioners also describe helping people who struggle with their sense of self or understanding of reality after psychedelic use <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Argyri et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These studies draw attention to distress and support needs, however, they do not show that spirituality caused the distress or establish spiritual emergency as a validated diagnosis.
A mixed-methods investigation based on three linked surveys found that users attributed both the emergence and resolution of spiritual struggles to psychedelics (Schutt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A mixed-methods investigation based on three linked surveys found that users attributed both the emergence and resolution of spiritual struggles to psychedelics <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Schutt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This finding matters for prevention because a difficult experience may be interpreted in more than one way and may change over time.
Follow-up should therefore record what difficulties people report, how long they last, whether they disrupt daily life, and whether a person can obtain help.
Finding later meaning or growth in an destabilizing experience does not mean that earlier distress should be dismissed.
Conversely, a brief period of distress does not necessarily indicate lasting harm.
Research should ask concrete questions.
Does describing distress as necessary spiritual growth delay access to care?
Can claims of spiritual authority make it harder for participants to refuse further participation or express an alternative point of view?
These are hypotheses to investigate, not established effects.
Follow-up should record duration, disruption to everyday life, pressure from others, and difficulty obtaining help.
Existing frameworks discuss consent, professional conduct, access, and accountability (McGuire et al., 2024; Spriggs et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Existing frameworks discuss consent, professional conduct, access, and accountability <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(McGuire et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Spriggs et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative research with practitioners across clinical, community, and ceremonial settings has also identified preparation, accountability, and ongoing support as concerns (Chwyl et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Qualitative research with practitioners across clinical, community, and ceremonial settings has also identified preparation, accountability, and ongoing support as concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chwyl et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These sources help identify protections to consider across settings, but their effectiveness remain to be tested.
Second, participants should have a way to report problems to someone outside the facilitator's authority.
This matters because participants may fear negative consequences or losing access to support if they complain or report a problem.
A clinical qualification or spiritual reputation cannot replace a functioning complaints process.
People should also be able to leave a group without losing access to independent help.
Third, help after the experience should be available independently of the original provider.
Confidentiality matters here because fear of exposure or punishment could discourage honest reporting.
A person who feels pressured by a facilitator or frightened by unwanted belief changes needs a credible way to report this without increasing their own vulnerability.
These protections need to fit the communities concerned.
Indigenous traditions involve shared responsibilities, knowledge, and relationships, therefore, they cannot be treated simply as services delivered to individual consumers.
Indigenous peoples should have a role in deciding how their traditions are represented and how external standards affect them (Spriggs et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Indigenous peoples should have a role in deciding how their traditions are represented and how external standards affect them <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Spriggs et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This means respecting their authority over their own knowledge and practices, as well as their role in shaping safeguards.
Cognitive liberty is an ethical argument for allowing people some freedom to explore their consciousness, while also protecting their ability to refuse unwanted influence (Walsh, 2016).
text.formatted: Cognitive liberty is an ethical argument for allowing people some freedom to explore their consciousness, while also protecting their ability to refuse unwanted influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Walsh, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: It is not a universally enforceable legal right to obtain controlled substances.
It does, however, give policymakers a reason to examine whether restrictions are necessary and whether they prevent coercion or create it.
Freedom of religion or belief provides a legal framework for considering religious uses.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee (1993, paras. 2-3, 8) distinguishes freedom to hold beliefs from religious practices, which may be subject to lawful, necessary and proportionate restrictions.
Thus, religious significance does not automatically exempt a psychedelic practice from regulation.
However, a safety requirement should have a defensible protective purpose rather than simply exclude an unfamiliar or alternative worldview.
The same concern for fairness extends to adults whose purposes are neither medical nor religious.
They may seek meaning, relationships, or personal exploration without claiming treatment or sacrament.
This does not mean that the law should assign different rules solely according to a person's stated intention.
It means that policy should explain why a practice or setting warrants a particular restriction, and should not assume that only medical or religious purposes are legitimate.

There is a serious argument for restricting some psychedelic services to settings with trained staff, emergency capacity, and enforceable standards, as some risks and populations may require clinical pathways.
Precaution can also be justified before the frequency of a serious adverse outcome is known precisely.
If a setting cannot protect participants adequately, tighter restrictions may be justified.
But if comparable protections can be provided in different settings, policymakers should explain why access must be limited to clinical services.

In other words, the policy question is whether a setting can provide the needed protections, not simply whether it is labelled clinical or spiritual. Mian et al. (2025) help distinguish different regulatory arrangements.
text.formatted: In other words, the policy question is whether a setting can provide the needed protections, not simply whether it is labelled clinical or spiritual. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Mian et al. (2025)</ref> help distinguish different regulatory arrangements.

text.text: For example, a community service could be required to screen for risks, respect consent and arrange emergency referral without presenting itself as psychiatric treatment.
Claims to treat a disorder would require separate evidence and oversight.
Asking which responsibilities require medical expertise makes the access debate more precise.
Prohibition must also be assessed by its consequences.

Indeed, even if penalties reduce drug use, this does not establish that their overall health and social consequences are beneficial. Scheim et al. (2020) The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (2023, para. 14) reports concern about barriers to treatment, stigma and exclusion associated with punitive drug policy.
text.formatted: Indeed, even if penalties reduce drug use, this does not establish that their overall health and social consequences are beneficial. <ref type="formula">Scheim et al. (2020)</ref> The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (2023, para. 14) reports concern about barriers to treatment, stigma and exclusion associated with punitive drug policy.

text.text: These concerns relate to drug policy broadly, rather than measured effects among psychedelic users, nevertheless, they justify considering policy-generated harms.
Removing possession penalties is different from authorising commercial supply.
Whatever the legal framework, people experiencing difficulties should have access to confidential information and support.
Prospective studies should begin before use and follow people across different settings.
They should assess previous beliefs, mental health, substance and dose, alongside support and subsequent exposure.
Studies should distinguish between participants who choose spiritual framewokrs and those who feel pressured by a facilitator to accept particular beliefs.
This would help investigate whether difficulties relate to the experience, unwanted influence, or their interaction.
Appropriate comparison groups and interviews with people reporting benefits, harms, or who stop participating after a difficult experience would strengthen interpretation.
Measures of spiritual bypassing and spiritual emergency also need validation in the populations studied.
They should assess avoidance, pressure or interpersonal consequences without assuming that spiritual identification is itself a problem.

Combining these measures with established assessments of symptoms and functioning would help identify difficulties that matter in daily life, including those missed by reports of personal growth alone.
Safeguards also need evaluation.
Does independent reporting make abuse easier to disclose?
Does access to outside support reduce prolonged distress?
Do licensing or training requirements improve protection, or make services unaffordable?
Standards can increase costs and potentially limit access for people with fewer financial resources (McGuire et al., 2024; Noorani, 2020).
text.formatted: Standards can increase costs and potentially limit access for people with fewer financial resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(McGuire et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Noorani, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Research should examine these costs alongside safety, and involve the people expected to use or provide support.
For many people, psychedelic experiences, and sometimes mystical experiences in particular, can be profoundly meaningful, beneficial and beautiful.
The same experiences may also create periods of unusual vulnerability.
Drug policy should therefore seek to protect people

People should know who is facilitating, what support is available, and whether spiritual teaching is part of the practice.
They should be able to ask questions, change their preferences, or refuse an activity.
Researchers and providers should check that participants understand these choices and that refusal is respected.
Some people may prefer peers or spiritual care while others need qualified mental-health assessment.
Services should explain what they can offer and arrange referral when needs exceed their competence.
Fourth, services and researchers should follow individual difficulties as carefully as average improvement.
Monitoring should distinguish symptom changes, everyday functioning, spiritual struggles and interpersonal harm, and record further substance use and other care.
